Writing a Dockerfile: Base images; core instructions; the build context

slides.title: Writing Images As Code
slides.lead: A Dockerfile is a plain-text script that Docker reads top to bottom to build an image automatically, instead of configuring a container by hand each time

points.text: Base image: the starting layer every Dockerfile selects first
Core instructions: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, EXPOSE, CMD build the image
Build context: the files and folders sent to the Docker daemon

slides.notes: "Frame the Dockerfile as a recipe the daemon follows exactly once, every time. Mention that each of the three parts gets its own slide next. Interview hook: a Dockerfile makes builds reproducible across machines."

slides.title: Starting Point Matters
slides.lead: A base image is the starting layer every instruction builds on: it fixes the operating system, runtime and tools already present before any custom code is added

points.text: Full distro images (ubuntu, debian): larger, many pre-installed utilities
Slim/alpine variants: smaller footprint, minimal shell and libraries

slides.notes: "Point out that the base image choice decides most of the final image's size and attack surface. Say the everyday version first: bigger base, more baggage. Exam hook: why slim or alpine images are often preferred for production, and where Alpine's musl libc can cause compatibility problems."

slides.title: Starting Point Matters

points.text: Official language images (python, node): runtime pre-installed, versioned tags
`scratch`: an empty base
Commonly used for fully static binaries or applications that include all required dependencies

slides.notes: "Point out that the base image choice decides most of the final image's size and attack surface. Say the everyday version first: bigger base, more baggage. Exam hook: why slim or alpine images are often preferred for production, and where Alpine's musl libc can cause compatibility problems."

slides.label: Analogy: a furnished house and a basic house
slides.title: Starting Point Matters
slides.notes: TR analogy: Picking a base image is like choosing a house for your needs: a fully furnished house comes with many facilities, while a basic house has only essential facilities, just as a full distro image includes many pre-installed tools, while a slim or alpine image includes only the essentials. "Point out that the base image choice decides most of the final image's size and attack surface. Say the everyday version first: bigger base, more baggage. Exam hook: why slim or alpine images are often preferred for production, and where Alpine's musl libc can cause compatibility problems."

slides.title: Six Key Keywords
slides.lead: Beyond selecting a base image and copying files, a Dockerfile needs instructions that set the working directory, run build-time commands and declare what starts the container

cells: Copies files from build context in
Executes a command, bakes result into layer

slides.notes: "Stress that, among these six, CMD is the only instruction that runs when the container starts, not when the image builds. Explain RUN bakes its output into a layer permanently. Exam hook: difference between RUN and CMD is a frequent interview question."

slides.title: What Daemon Receives
slides.lead: Running a build sends the build context, the folder named at the end of the docker build command (usually . for the current folder), to the Docker builder, so every COPY instruction can only reach files inside it

points.text: Context size: large folders slow every build, even unrelated changes
`.dockerignore`: excludes files like `.git` or `node_modules` from context

slides.notes: "Explain that an oversized context is a common cause of slow builds even when code barely changed. Point to .dockerignore as the direct fix. Exam hook: ask why a build fails to find a file placed outside its folder."

slides.title: What Daemon Receives

points.text: COPY path error: a file outside context cannot be copied in
Context root: set by the trailing dot in the build command

slides.notes: "Explain that an oversized context is a common cause of slow builds even when code barely changed. Point to .dockerignore as the direct fix. Exam hook: ask why a build fails to find a file placed outside its folder."
Layers & Caching: Layer creation & reuse; instruction ordering for cache efficiency

slides.title: What Changes Here
slides.lead: Every filesystem-changing instruction in a Dockerfile creates a read-only layer, and Docker can reuse a layer only when nothing it depends on has changed

points.text: Layer creation: RUN, COPY and ADD each add a layer; ENV, EXPOSE and CMD add only metadata
Layer sharing: layers are read-only, so images built from the same base reuse the same stored layers

slides.notes: "Recall that each instruction builds on the layer before it. Ask: which instructions in the practical Dockerfile create layers? Interview hook: explain Docker's cache-hit condition precisely."

slides.title: What Changes Here

points.text: Layer count: Combining related commands into one RUN instruction can reduce the number of layers and keep the image smaller
Cache reuse: an unchanged layer is taken from the cache instead of being rebuilt

slides.notes: "Recall that each instruction builds on the layer before it. Ask: which instructions in the practical Dockerfile create layers? Interview hook: explain Docker's cache-hit condition precisely."

slides.title: Checksum And Cascade
slides.lead: Docker computes a checksum for each instruction and the files it touches, comparing it against the checksum stored with the existing layer

points.text: Matching checksum on both sides reuses the stored layer untouched
Any mismatch rebuilds that layer; a broad COPY . . changes whenever any file in the context changes

slides.notes: "Point out that the cascade, not the single layer, is what makes ordering matter — this is the mechanism behind the earlier FROM/COPY/EXPOSE example. Common interview question: why does changing line 2 of a Dockerfile rebuild line 3 even if line 3 is unchanged."

slides.title: Checksum And Cascade

points.text: When a layer changes, that layer and every layer after it must be rebuilt
Build output marks a reused layer as CACHED in the logs

slides.notes: "Point out that the cascade, not the single layer, is what makes ordering matter — this is the mechanism behind the earlier FROM/COPY/EXPOSE example. Common interview question: why does changing line 2 of a Dockerfile rebuild line 3 even if line 3 is unchanged."

slides.title: Dependency Before Code
slides.lead: Because a cache miss cascades downward, the cascade should be triggered as late as possible: rarely-changing instructions go first, frequently-changing ones last

points.text: Copy the dependency manifest file before the application source
Install dependencies in their own layer, which rarely invalidates

slides.notes: "Explain that this is exactly why manifest files are copied ahead of source code in real builds — dependency installs are the expensive step to protect from invalidation. Exam hook: ask what rebuilds if only the application file changes under this ordering."

slides.title: Dependency Before Code

points.text: Copy application code last, since it changes on nearly every build
`docker build --no-cache` forces a full rebuild when needed

slides.notes: "Explain that this is exactly why manifest files are copied ahead of source code in real builds — dependency installs are the expensive step to protect from invalidation. Exam hook: ask what rebuilds if only the application file changes under this ordering."
Image Optimization: Minimal base images; multi-stage builds; image size & attack surface

slides.title: Three Levers
slides.lead: An unoptimized image still ships unnecessary packages inside every layer, which slows every pull and expands what an attacker can target

points.text: Minimal base images: start from the smallest OS that still runs the app
Multi-stage builds: separate the build toolchain from the shipped runtime
Trimmed attack surface: fewer packages means fewer exploitable vulnerabilities

slides.notes: "Frame image optimization as three separate levers, not one technique. Ask why a smaller image also means a smaller attack surface. Stress that this builds directly on container layering."

slides.title: Smaller OS Footprint
slides.lead: A minimal base image contains only the essential operating-system components, libraries and dependencies needed to run an application, instead of including unnecessary tools and packages

points.text: Full distributions bundle shells, editors and compilers unused at runtime
Alpine Linux uses musl libc and busybox for a far smaller footprint

slides.notes: "Explain minimal base images using the kitchen picture, then name Alpine and distroless as the two common choices. Contrast slim variants as a middle ground between a full OS and distroless. Interview angle: why not always use distroless?"

slides.title: Smaller OS Footprint

points.text: Distroless images remove the shell and package manager entirely
Trade-off: Alpine's musl libc can break software built for glibc
And distroless images cannot be debugged with a shell

slides.notes: "Explain minimal base images using the kitchen picture, then name Alpine and distroless as the two common choices. Contrast slim variants as a middle ground between a full OS and distroless. Interview angle: why not always use distroless?"

slides.label: Analogy: packing for a short trip
slides.title: Smaller OS Footprint
slides.notes: TR analogy: Packing for a short trip requires only the clothes and items you need, not your entire wardrobe, just as a minimal base image contains only the essential components needed to run an application, without unnecessary tools and packages. "Explain minimal base images using the kitchen picture, then name Alpine and distroless as the two common choices. Contrast slim variants as a middle ground between a full OS and distroless. Interview angle: why not always use distroless?"

slides.title: Build Then Ship
slides.lead: A single-stage Dockerfile that compiles and runs code ships the whole build toolchain inside the final image, even though runtime never uses it

points.text: Build stage installs dependencies and compiles the app with the full toolchain
Final stage copies only the compiled output into a clean runtime image

slides.notes: "Trace the two FROM lines: first builds, second ships. Emphasise only the last stage becomes the final image, so compilers never reach production."

slides.title: Build Then Ship

points.text: `COPY --from=build` copies only compiled output, never source or tools

slides.notes: "Trace the two FROM lines: first builds, second ships. Emphasise only the last stage becomes the final image, so compilers never reach production."

slides.title: Base Image Compared
slides.lead: Smaller images generally have a smaller attack surface because they contain fewer packages and components that need patching and could be exploited
slides.notes: "Walk down the table noting size tier drops as the package manager and shell disappear. Point out distroless trades debugging convenience for the smallest attack surface. Interview hook: why can a shell not be used to debug a distroless container?"

slides.title: Base Image Compared
slides.notes: "Walk down the table noting size tier drops as the package manager and shell disappear. Point out distroless trades debugging convenience for the smallest attack surface. Interview hook: why can a shell not be used to debug a distroless container?"

slides.title: Scanning And Scope
slides.lead: A registry such as Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry) can scan a pushed image for known vulnerabilities, and a smaller image surfaces far fewer findings to fix

points.text: When turned on, ECR image scanning flags CVEs in installed packages
Multi-stage builds and minimal bases together cut both size and findings
Smaller images also pull faster across orchestration clusters

slides.notes: "Name ECR scanning as where this choice shows up in the console, not just in theory. Tie smaller images to faster pulls and fewer CVE findings as the real payoff. Exam hook: why does reducing attack surface also reduce scan findings?"
Container Configuration: Environment variables, volumes & port mapping; secrets handling

slides.title: Four Config Levers
slides.lead: A container image stays generic until runtime settings make it fit one environment, extending the twelve-factor idea of keeping config outside code

points.text: Environment variables: inject settings at start-up without changing the image
Volumes: attach storage that outlives the container
Port mapping: expose a container's service to the host
Secrets handling: supply credentials without baking them into the image

slides.notes: "State that these four levers turn one built image into many deployable instances. Point at each arrow while naming it. Ask: why must configuration live outside the image rather than inside it?"

slides.title: Runtime Config Injection
slides.lead: A container image can contain default settings, while environment variables injected at runtime allow the same image to behave differently in each environment

points.text: ENV in a Dockerfile sets a default value inside the image
Application code reads the variable, for example via `getenv`
Missing variable falls back to a default string coded in the app

slides.notes: "Explain that -e overrides any ENV default baked into the image. Mention getenv() as the code-side read. Ask how an app's displayed message can change without rebuilding the image."

slides.label: Analogy: phone settings changed per user
slides.title: Runtime Config Injection
slides.notes: TR analogy: A mobile phone comes with default settings, but each user can change the language or brightness based on their preference, just as the same container image can use different environment variable values in different environments. "Explain that -e overrides any ENV default baked into the image. Mention getenv() as the code-side read. Ask how an app's displayed message can change without rebuilding the image."

slides.title: Storage And Networking
slides.lead: Container storage disappears when a container is removed, and its network stays isolated by default; volumes and port mapping are the two fixes for that

cells: Portable storage, decoupled from host path
Direct host path, live-edit during development

slides.notes: "Walk through the -p 8080:5000 syntax on screen and contrast it with a bind mount's host path. Ask the difference between EXPOSE and -p, a common interview question."

slides.title: Storage And Networking

points.text: `-v volumeName:/container/path` mounts a named volume into the container
`-p hostPort:containerPort` forwards host traffic to the container port

slides.notes: "Walk through the -p 8080:5000 syntax on screen and contrast it with a bind mount's host path. Ask the difference between EXPOSE and -p, a common interview question."

slides.title: Storage And Networking

points.text: Omitting the host port picks a random free host port
EXPOSE only documents the intended listening port

slides.notes: "Walk through the -p 8080:5000 syntax on screen and contrast it with a bind mount's host path. Ask the difference between EXPOSE and -p, a common interview question."

slides.title: Storage And Networking

points.text: `-p` is the docker run flag that actually publishes that port
Multiple containers can map different host ports to one image

slides.notes: "Walk through the -p 8080:5000 syntax on screen and contrast it with a bind mount's host path. Ask the difference between EXPOSE and -p, a common interview question."

slides.title: Beyond Env Variables
slides.lead: Environment variables are visible through docker inspect and process listings, so a password or API key placed there stays exposed to anyone with container access

points.text: Never hardcode secrets in a Dockerfile
A hardcoded secret persists permanently in the image layers

slides.notes: "Point out that docker inspect can reveal environment variables, which is why secrets need a different path. Name AWS Secrets Manager as the concrete service. Ask why ENV is unsafe for credentials despite being fine for config."

slides.title: Beyond Env Variables

points.text: Mounted secret files keep credentials out of environment and image history
Managed secret stores, such as AWS Secrets Manager, inject values at runtime
Secrets rotate independently of the image, with no rebuild needed

slides.notes: "Point out that docker inspect can reveal environment variables, which is why secrets need a different path. Name AWS Secrets Manager as the concrete service. Ask why ENV is unsafe for credentials despite being fine for config."
Multi-Container Apps & Registries: Compose: services, networks & dependencies; push & pull; tagging strategy & immutable tags

slides.title: Compose And Registries
slides.lead:
A real application rarely runs as one container; a web service, a database and a cache must start together and reach each other
Sharing a built image across machines then needs a third piece: a registry workflow

points.text: Docker Compose: one file defining several linked services
Push and pull: moving an image to and from a registry
Tagging strategy: naming versions so the right build is found

slides.notes: "Frame this as the natural next step after single-container Docker: real apps need several containers coordinated, and images need a cloud home. Ask: why can't one Dockerfile alone run a web app plus its database?"

slides.title: One File Many Services
slides.lead:
Starting a web container and a database container with separate docker run commands is error-prone
Docker Compose, a tool that describes multiple containers as services in one YAML file, starts the whole application together

points.text: Each service names an image or a build context
`compose.yaml` is the default filename Compose reads

slides.notes: "Say Compose replaces several manual docker run commands with one declarative file. Point to the services key as the anchor every learner should look for first. Interview angle: ask why Compose matters for local multi-service development."

slides.title: One File Many Services

points.text: `docker compose up -d` starts all services in the background
`docker compose down` stops and removes the whole group

slides.notes: "Say Compose replaces several manual docker run commands with one declarative file. Point to the services key as the anchor every learner should look for first. Interview angle: ask why Compose matters for local multi-service development."

slides.label: Analogy: a school timetable
slides.title: One File Many Services
slides.notes: TR analogy: A school timetable coordinates different classes and teachers to run together smoothly, just as Docker Compose manages multiple services from one file. "Say Compose replaces several manual docker run commands with one declarative file. Point to the services key as the anchor every learner should look for first. Interview angle: ask why Compose matters for local multi-service development."

slides.title: Service Communication
slides.lead: Services in one Compose file need to find each other without hardcoded addresses, and some must wait for another to be ready first

points.text: Default network: Compose joins all services to one shared network
Service name as hostname: web reaches db at `db:5432`

slides.notes: "Explain that the service name itself works as a DNS hostname inside the shared network, so no IP address is ever hardcoded. Mention depends_on only orders container start, not application readiness, as a common interview trap."

slides.title: Service Communication

points.text: depends_on: sets start order; service_healthy waits for readiness
Custom networks: isolate a group of services from the rest

slides.notes: "Explain that the service name itself works as a DNS hostname inside the shared network, so no IP address is ever hardcoded. Mention depends_on only orders container start, not application readiness, as a common interview trap."

slides.title: Two Linked Services
slides.lead: A two-service file shows how the web application and its database are declared and wired together in practice

points.text: web is built from the local Dockerfile and waits for db to start first
db runs the official `postgres:16` image
With its password read from the `DB_PASSWORD` variable instead of being written in the file

slides.notes: "Walk through build versus image: web is built locally, db pulls a ready image. Point out port 80 on the host mapping to the container's 5000, same pattern as a single-container run."

slides.title: Publishing An Image
slides.lead: A locally built image stays on one machine until it is tagged for a registry address and pushed; another machine then pulls the identical bytes back down

points.text: Login: authenticate to the registry before pushing (ECR login tokens last 12 hours)

Tag: rename the image as
`registry-address/repository:tag`

slides.notes: "Emphasise the layer-by-layer transfer: only changed layers move, which is why repeated pushes of a similar image are fast. Mention a cloud registry such as Amazon ECR as where this exact flow happens."

slides.title: Publishing An Image

points.text: Push: uploads only the image layers the registry lacks
Pull: downloads only the layers missing from the local cache

slides.notes: "Emphasise the layer-by-layer transfer: only changed layers move, which is why repeated pushes of a similar image are fast. Mention a cloud registry such as Amazon ECR as where this exact flow happens."

slides.title: Registry-Level Immutability
slides.lead:
A mutable tag can silently start pointing at a different image after a later push, so redeploying the same tag months later may run an unexpected build
Registries let an owner lock a tag against this

points.text: Tag immutability setting: repository refuses to re-push an existing tag
Digest pinning: a deployment refers to the sha256 digest directly

slides.notes: "Explain this goes beyond naming a tag: the registry itself can enforce that a tag never changes once pushed. A common interview question is why production pipelines pin a digest instead of trusting a tag alone."

slides.title: Registry-Level Immutability

points.text: Reproducibility: a locked tag always resolves to one exact image
Rollback safety: an immutable tag always redeploys the exact same image

slides.notes: "Explain this goes beyond naming a tag: the registry itself can enforce that a tag never changes once pushed. A common interview question is why production pipelines pin a digest instead of trusting a tag alone."

slides.title: Choosing A Scheme
slides.lead: Different tagging choices trade convenience for certainty about exactly which image gets run
slides.notes: "Walk left to right: latest is fine for a laptop, but production always moves to a locked tag or a digest. Point out that the three rows map directly onto the deployment and rollback decisions made earlier."
